utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today, is Monday, the 30th of June, 2008. My greetings to the witness first, who's going to start testifying in a few minutes. Good afternoon to the Defence counsel, the accused, the OTP representatives, and all the people helping us out. Witness, can you please state your first name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Slobodan Jankovic. I was born on the 10th of August, 1932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Well, I can hear you speak French. Thank you for that. Can you please tell me what is your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a retired university professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you had an opportunity to testify before a court; if so, in which case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a witness here as an expert witness on two occasions, in the Blaskic case first and then in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified before a domestic court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, throughout my career I was an expert on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, sir, some explanation on the way the hearing is going to take place. As you have been a witness on two occasions in the Blaskic and Kordic cases, I'm not going to surprise you in saying what I'm about to say. You will first have to answer questions by the Defence of General Praljak. I suppose you've met his counsel, Mr. Kovacic, prior to this hearing. The overall time scheduled is one hour for those questions. Following this part of the proceedings, the other Defence counsel sitting on your left-hand side can also ask questions of you. We have decided to grant them 50 per cent of their time, that is 30 minutes, if they have questions to put as part of their own cross-examination. Thereafter, the Office of the Prosecutor, represented by the two people sitting on your right-hand side will ask questions as part of their cross-examination and they will have one hour and 30 minutes to do so. You have four Judges in front of you. I'm sure they're bound to ask questions themselves based on the evidence submitted through your answers, following questions by all the parties. You're a professor, as such you know very well that you have to be very concise in your answers. If you fail to understand the meaning of a question, do not hesitate, ask the person asking you the question to rephrase it. We usually break every 90 minutes for 30 -- for 20 minutes; but if you do not feel well, if you wish to have a short break, just raise your right hand and we'll have a break straight away. That can happen. We've known instances such as that. Of course the Trial Chamber is available to you should you have questions for the Judges. You have just made a solemn declaration; that means that from now on you are a witness of justice of the Court. You're no longer a witness of General Praljak's Defence, since your oath commits yourself to tell the truth and you are a witness of justice. In other words, if we fail to finish today, if we have to carry on your testimony tomorrow, you're not supposed to have any contact with General Praljak's Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I wanted to convey to you before I give the floor to Mr. Kovacic. But before I do so I forgot that our registrar has two IC numbers to give us. Can you give them to us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two lists of documents tendered through Witness Zarko Primorac. Prlic Defence list will become Exhibit IC 818, and Prosecution list will become Exhibit IC 819. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Kovacic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I thank you for allowing me to start. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. A very good afternoon to Mr. Jankovic, Professor Jankovic. I thank you for coming here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, I will be addressing you as Professor Jankovic, I think that is appropriate, in view of your status.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the thing that is usually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Professor, just for your own comfort, I'm not sure if you've been told, you could use channel 5 to listen to the French and channel 6 to listen to the Croatian, so whichever you like best. Secondly, you're apparently willing to testify in French. We're only too glad to have you go ahead with that, especially for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. This will be much better in terms of us being able to avoid technical difficulties and misunderstandings. So you want to go on and testify in French, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During the introduction by the Presiding Judge you mentioned that you have already testified before domestic courts, national courts, as an expert. A question about that, because our system is different, just to make sure the Chamber understands. Where we come from, experts are given permanent status with a certain Tribunal or court, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear. Thank you. And you testified at several trials, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you several questions about your CV, since you appear here as an expert, just to try to demonstrate your professional qualifications. With the approval of the Chamber and with the agreement of my learned friends I would try to lead the witness here because this might prove to be very time-saving. Professor, based on your CV you were born in Brussels, you went to the Polytechnic in Brussels and then the applied school of artillery, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, a degree in civilian -- in civil engineering to do with weapons would be a civilian equivalent of this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, Witness, you have to wait before answering because the interpreters work from two booths and they have to wait. So when Mr. Kovacic is finished, you have to count until five and then you can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. This is my mistake. I was hurrying along in a bid to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is civil engineering with a specialty in weaponry, that would be the civilian equivalent, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then your graduate studies in Belgrade in 1964, the engineering faculty in Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I graduated from the school of mathematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then in 1968 you took your Ph.D. in Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: In the school of mechanics, civil engineering -- mechanical engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about your work after that, was it flight mechanics and aero mechanics?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After that, sir, Professor Jankovic - and I'll try to save time here - you worked with the army, with the institute for development specifically, other sectors of the army too, but you spent most of your time there. You worked in the country's industry and you worked at both civilian and military faculties as a professor, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It is exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, you published a lot of articles, works of research. I think over 40 if my count is correct, in addition to which you published six books from your own field of research, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your last important work was published at an important international ballistics conference in San Antonio in the USA in 2000, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From the early 1990s on, you have been working with the ship-building institute in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I would add that that year I retired, but the Croatian army recalled me because they needed me and I worked then in that institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Some people may not know Zagreb or its institutions. Can you please explain in a couple of words what this institute is because the name itself does not really tell us what it is. Can you please so kind as to explain in no more than a couple of words the nature of this institution?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1990, the institute was mainly working on boat-building, but then when there was a change in states, when there was a new Croatia, that institute became a technical institute, taking in -- taking charge of all complicated projects and that's why they called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Before it disappears, I believe that I heard that the San Antonio conference was in 2004, whilst I see on lines 7 and 8 2000, not 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's reflected in the record is correct, Your Honour, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, in addition to all of this you are also a consultant with a recently established state agency, which in a way promotes scientific projects, particularly those of a multi-disciplinary nature and it promotes the work of young scientists. Can you tell us briefly what the work of this institution is about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a parliament agency whose purpose is to help new companies when they develop intricate projects through funding. I am a consultant inasmuch as a project will first arrive in my office and then I'll give an opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is quite sufficient as far as your scientific background is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If no one has a problem and if Your Honours have no further questions to ask, I'd like to move on to my next subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we're looking into your professional achievements, it seems that you were a JNA officer. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was an officer, an active JNA officer. Once I finished my studies in Brussels at the Polytechnical School and in the applied school until 1972. Then I left the active service, but I remained as a scientist as part of the army but as a civilian scientist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was your rank when you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just to put a question. What was your service, what was your specialty in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technical service, but mainly for artillery questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to our next subject. Professor, you were working with a number of people, we will get to that later who exactly, and you drew up an opinion at the request of General Praljak, it's called: "The analysis of the destruction of the Old Bridge based on available video footage." January 2006 is the date of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, we submitted this document on the 9th of May. The number is 3D 03208. Professor, bearing in mind the nature of this type of research, is this a job that requires a multi-disciplinary approach?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever we have to examine a technical event that took place somewhere, it is a complicated process. Many disciplines are involved in the event. That's quite normal. Because of that, more often than not, we'll work as a team, not as individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video 3D 03208, do you plan to show it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we'll soon be getting to that. It has two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, just to make sure my understanding is correct does this mean that in addition to your general experience as an engineer in various fields you needed to use your specialist knowledge as well in a variety of different fields in order to deal with the task you were facing?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, it is always the case whenever we examine past technical events we need to have very advanced knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, try and avoid putting leading questions. This one was a tiny bit leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree that this is a leading question, Your Honour, but this is still part of my introduction and that's why I took the liberty. I will now be coming to a section of my examination where I will no longer be asking leading questions. Thank you very much for the caution anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, we have established that the analysis was written up by an entire team of people working on it. Can you tell us about the other members of this team, their names and their fields of research?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these are two colleagues I used to work with at the institute, at the boat-building institute, they are Aleksandar Sikanic, he is a projectile builder, that's the reason why I invited him on to the team; and the other is Suceska, he's an explosive specialist, since this was also an event concerned with explosives, so I invited him too. And we worked as a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, you've broached the topic in reply to one of my previous questions, but let's try to be more specific about it. Is there any other reason, aside from purely specialised knowledge, why a project like this would be tackled by an entire team of people? Does this broaden or deepen our understanding of any particular technical issue involved?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: It's always a good thing to have a team because you can exchange views; you know, the more there are, the more we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's try to be even more specific. You work on this project and then a question arises, for example, someone comes up with a theory. Does group work yield better results in these terms? Does it make it easier to study a given theory just because there are several different points of view involved in this research? Does that corroborate any conclusions that are reached even more than individual work might?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. If a problem crops up, we'll discuss it, we'll thrash it out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Professor. The Prosecution is on its feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My name again is Kim West. I just recently joined the OTP and I'll be handling the cross-examination of this witness. I would just point out for the Chamber that I think counsel is now again getting into a leading question, and I would just ask that the questions be open-ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic, do endeavour not to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. I do admit that this was a leading question to some extent. I didn't feel that the topic was particularly sensitive, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps to save a minute or two, Professor, as for Dr. Muhamed Suceska and Dr. Aco Sikanic, they were your partners on this project. Just for the benefit of the transcript, let me say this: The documents were distributed to the parties, 3D 03220, and Professor Sikanic, 3D 03221. Professor, these documents were attached to your analysis, as you know. Do you agree that the curricula of your fellow researchers are accurate? You can go back to that folder that you've got. I believe you leafed through it already. These are the third and fourth documents in your folder.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. No need to look at the documents. I know these people. They are professors as well. They are doctors in sciences. They are very competent people, very knowledgeable in their fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to move on to the next topic, unless the Trial Chamber has any questions. I would now like to move on to the analysis itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the curricula, just one question. Professor, I haven't had time - please forgive me for that - to read all your publications and those by your excellent colleague Mr. Suceska, but I'm under the impression - and please correct me if I'm wrong - my impression is that you -- you are a specialist in projectiles, missiles, and any other means of carrying explosives, that is your main expertise; whilst Professor Suceska, from a very cursory examination of his articles, seems to be a specialist in what is in the missile or about the core of the explosive charge. So he seemed to be more of a specialist in explosives, and you together -- well, you are sort of complementary, him and you. Am I wrong? Please correct me if I am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you're not wrong, but I could also add something. I studied at Ecole Polytechnique, so my knowledge encompasses all these issues. Since we were dealing with explosives, I thought it was better to have a specialist on board for very detailed problems because when you sort of have a broad approach you may forget details. And third thing, we invited Sikanic onto the team because he builds projectiles, so he's aware of details -- well, I know that matter as well very well, but you have to know the weaponry and all the details pertaining to them. You need to have all the information. So as a team we could encompass everything and we also knew right into the details, which we needed when it came to this analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the analysis itself, for the record, was assigned number 3D 03208. You have it in front of you, Professor. My first question to you was: What was the task? What was this expert opinion all about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, we received the recordings and we were asked to deliver an opinion. Indeed, until then the only accepted truth was that the bridge had been destroyed by a tank, and we were asked to see whether we could confirm that or not through our analysis. That was our starting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, prior to the hearing I was thinking of this -- well, the tank. We may see some video recordings of a tank firing at the bridge. Of course Judges cannot sort of master all the evidence because we depend on evidence adduced by the parties, but from memory I seem to remember that the crew of the tank were subject to disciplinary proceedings following the firing. Could you have access to the files arising from the disciplinary proceedings against the tank crew or could you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't know anything about it. We couldn't access them. The only thing we had were the recordings and our conclusions, our findings, are based solely on the recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So having done this analysis - and we see the results here in the form of this report - what was the main conclusion of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Shall I go straight to the conclusion then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I propose that we go back and deal with the details later, but now I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's me, Your Honour, I was -- I was checking something shortly before the trial and I forget. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I hope that you're not going to get the conclusion through your telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but I have problems switching it off completely to be quite honest with you. [In English] I didn't do that much before the trial, but this time I was checking whether the witness was here, et cetera. [Interpretation] Once again, my apologies to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So bearing in mind the task that was given to you, let us now go into conclusions as a whole but could you please give us the key, the main conclusion that answers the question that was defined in the task. So what was the conclusion of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Without explaining how we arrived at the conclusion, here was the conclusion. It is highly probable that the bridge was destroyed by an explosive charge, that was our final conclusion; but I would like to explain how we got there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Kovacic, but I'd like to ask a question about terminology of the witness. Now, you speak about destruction, but there is another term that is "ecroulement," collapse, are they synonymous in your mind or do you think there's a difference ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a rather tricky question, a tough one. I'd like to answer your question with the video recordings. When I mention collapse, I think that the bridge would fall into the water; and if I speak of destruction, well, the bridge is destroyed, it no longer exists. That would be my thought. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's remain with semantics. Must there be first destruction and then collapse, or can both happen together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would say that the bridge is destroyed after it has collapsed. There is first collapse and then destruction. It collapsed, therefore it is destroyed. But it may be that my French is not good enough but that's how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether Judge Mindua wants to ask the same question. I'll give him the right of way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, let's talk about the process. Destruction is the final result, and collapse, that's the event.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. That's exactly that. Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it may be that my question is a little thornier. Now, does your answer imply that if there's no collapse there's no destruction? Does your answer mean that if there's no collapse there's no destruction? Is that what you mean? Is that so? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there is collapse there is destruction, but there can be other destruction also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I hope that this has been helpful. Bearing in mind that you have explained in your answers that your analysis was based on the available video materials, that's noted in the title itself of the paper that you wrote, I would like to ask you to describe what video materials were available and what materials you used to do this analysis.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: We were given several recordings, amongst which there were two in relation to those events. The first recording came from the Austrian TV, TV ORF2; as for the second recording, it came from TV Mostar. So those were the two recordings that we analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask my associate to play the ORF2 recording and then the other one so that you could confirm that those were the two video recordings that you were dealing with in your analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We saw two short segments. Could you identify and confirm that the first one is the ORF2 material, as we call it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And could you please confirm that the second one is the so-called Mostar video?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have IC numbers for the two clips that we saw, the first and the second video-clip, for technical reasons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first video will become Exhibit IC 820, and the second video will become Exhibit IC 821. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So your analysis is based on these materials, as we learned from your answers. There is reference to a third video recording in your analysis. Could you please explain to us what is the third video-clip, why and how it was done.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The third video-clip was a recording of our experiment, an experiment which we made in order, first of all, to confirm our assumption; and secondly, to confirm certain elements for your purposes. In our opinion as specialists we didn't need that experiment, but we wanted to show to other people that a comparison could be made which would allow us to understand better what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Fine. Now I would like to ask my associate to play the third video-clip so that you could identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have an IC number for this video recording too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you give an exhibit number to the third video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit IC 822. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And this brings us to the very essence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a small question. As for the third video-clip, we saw the same event twice -- one event twice. Was it the same video that we saw twice or was that a video with two sequences?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you saw the same footage twice because the clip lasts for only a couple of seconds and the professor would come back to it later. The only reason why we played it now was to identify the clips because it says in the title of the paper that it -- the analysis was done on the basis of available video material so we just wanted to identify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you just mentioned three video recordings, the first one is IC 820. Was that recording shot by the Austrian TV ORF2? The second video, IC 821, was made by TV Mostar. As for the third video, IC 822, this one was a recording for our purposes. But it seems to me that during the testimony of one witness we saw a video, and on that shooting we saw balls, the bridge collapsed, and there was a water gush rising above the water. In the first two video-clips I didn't quite clearly see that. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are other recordings, but if I'm not mistaken, we've seen in this courtroom sections of 821 and of 820, the Mostar video and ORF respectively; and now we've played just a critical portion, the destruction, the collapse of the bridge that is at the core of what the Professor analysed. So they are not interested in what happened before and what happened later, they only analysed the critical moments. But yes, at least one of those recordings have been seen in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me I would like to ask a follow-up question. Professor, we saw three video-clips which lasted a few seconds each. Besides those clips, have you seen other footage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have. I have seen many, in fact, but we did not need them. They were not useful for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, maybe we will view those recordings later, but personally, I would like very much to see the footage with tracer bullets. On that video we can hear the tanks firing, we can see the bridge collapsing, but what is particularly important is that we see a water pillar vertically to the direction of the bridge. And I think this should be asked -- this should be put to the witness. Maybe we will have time enough to see that video, but in any case I would very much like to see that video again, a video which we have already seen on a couple of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kovacic, I see that the translation - and it's not an accident that I'm turning to English - the translation speaks of a pillar, a water pillar. The President has said a "mur d'eau" which would be a wall of water rather than a pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Trechsel. Yes, I understand that it is in reference to the same phenomenon, so there is no confusion here. But to answer, Mr. President, if you allow me with regard to what you said about water plume or the water wall, you will see this part soon because this is the very essence of the expert analysis and we will see this several times so that everybody has a good chance to see it. We will come to it soon enough. But as regards your second request, indicating that you would like to see what we have seen in this courtroom before again, the shelling of the bridge, the artillery shells, as we have been told; but with all due respect - and my associates may correct me if I'm wrong - we don't have it here with us but we will be able to produce it, I'm sure, after the break. But for the time being, I propose that we do it this way. You will be able to see it later, and I'm sure that the Professor will be able to explain to us why the video starts at a certain point. If you allow me, I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, I think this would be the most efficient way to proceed. Could you please explain in broad-brush strokes how you did your analysis, the methodology that you used, and the most important thing how and why you reached the conclusion that we have already mentioned here today. So I'm not going to be asking you questions, but I'm going to let you use your own words.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My associates --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My associates tell me that the registry does have copies of all the videos that were mentioned and that we saw earlier, but at any rate we can make a short break and then we will retrieve one of those but I don't think it will be necessary. But we'll see how -- we'll see that as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But, Professor Jankovic, at any rate, please do continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, as far as the technique goes, I remember that the three of us worked together all the time. Whenever we drew a conclusion, this conclusion was the result of our exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, could you please switch off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Switch the microphone off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the subject I will drop all the technical details which are included in our report. I will try and explain to you how we drew our conclusions. First of all, we try and figured out how the tank could have destroyed the bridge because there was a 100-millimetre gun on this gun and we knew that every projectile was half a kilo, and that was not sufficient to destroy a stone bridge. Several shots would have been necessary to destroy this bridge because all the shells cannot fall, impact, on the same place. So the distance would have been a circle of 1 metre -- the diameter would have been 1 metre. I think we have a problem with the translation. I need to stop now and -- the distance was 1.400 metres. If the gun fires always at the same point, if the aim is always the same, the tank cannot hit always the same point; but if the fire elements are not modified, the radius would be 1 metre. So you would have to fire several shells in order to make a dent in the bridge so that it collapses. That's what we were looking for, and we could not find it anywhere in the recordings. We could see that the tank was firing, that there was damage, but sometimes the tank would fire in one corner and then in another corner. So the firing did not aim always at the same point, not to the point where it could create a dent in the bridge. In such a case, five or six shots within a radius of 1 metre would have been necessary, but we have not seen that; therefore, we could not conclude that the bridge had been destroyed by the tank. Furthermore, if you consider the speed of the projectiles, about 700 metres per second, and in view of the number of shots per second by the TV cameras, every time that there is firing it can be seen and recorded. Therefore, the camera which recorded the collapsing of the bridge probably had the projectile in the previous frames, but we were not able to see that. We haven't found it. In view of those two elements we concluded that even though we do not know the reason for the collapse for sure, we could conclude that the bridge didn't collapse because of the projectiles. The bridge was damaged, nobody questions that; but as you mentioned, Your Honour, we saw a water gush or a water pillar, you call it a water wall. We were able to explain what was the reason for that. We see it on two recordings, the recordings made by TV Mostar and the recordings made by ORF2. The only explanation to us was that there was a detonating cord underneath the water. This cord was ignited, and the gas liberated by the explosion were such that the water rose. We needed to verify the situation, even though it was clear to us, but we wanted to show that there was a detonating cord. That's the reason why we did that experiment on a lake. We positioned a cord underneath the water, we ignited it, and we saw that there was this same water wall which I call a water pillar. In slow motion -- you should see in slow motion the recordings made by ORF2 and then the recordings of our experiment, both should be seen in slow motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we move to another subject, as you can imagine I was listening to you very carefully. The destruction of the Old Bridge is very important in the indictment. Furthermore, it has a symbolical importance. It is therefore very important that the Bench doesn't make mistakes as to what really happened. I was listening to you very carefully, and I have noticed that you just stated that the tank gun had 100-millimetre calibre. This tank could only fire shells weighing one and a half kilo. Therefore, a shell which hits the bridge weighs 1500 grams. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat what I said. It was a T-55 tank. This T-55 tank had a 100-millimetre calibre gun. This gun can use several types of projectiles, piercing shells, all the types of shells, I cannot remember how they're called, I don't use them, and there are also explosive shells. Those explosive shells weigh some 15 kilos, 200 grams. That is the weight of the projectile. Within the projectile you have an explosive charge which weighs one and a half kilos approximately, 1.46 kilogrammes. That is the explosive charge which destroys the aim, the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This explosive charge weighs 1.6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, 1.46 kilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the explosive charge can only hit the bridge within a diameter of one metre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, let me explain. I have to enter into details. That explosive shell is not designed to destroy or pierce the bridge; its aim is to kill people, kill the enemy. It was used in that case, but I do not know why. That projectile was not meant to pierce, it was not the right kind of ammunition to destroy the bridge. If we want to be precise, that gun was designed at fighting against other tanks. That's why you have those piercing shells. And explosive shells can be used as well if there are enemy forces around the tank. That's the first thing. This explosive shell which was used in that case, I have seen those too, I have seen those recordings. That projectile could not have pierced the stonewall. It could damage it and then explode. There could have been a dent in the wall, but in order to pierce the whole wall you need several shells. So there is a dispersion of the impacts on the wall. But if the elements remain the same for the projectiles, dispersion occurs in a diameter of approximately 1 metre. If you hit that stonewall, you have the bridge and you have the wall, if you hit that wall with a few projectiles, let's say five or six, you can pierce the wall or you can make a dent in the wall, a breach in the wall, and then the bridge will collapse; that's possible. But I haven't seen those projectiles. I haven't seen the projectiles being shot with the same elements in such a way that could have make the bridge to collapse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we have heard witnesses explaining that the tank fired for a protracted period of time. So mathematically speaking, in view of the accumulation of explosive charges fired at the bridge, wasn't there a breach at some point that could have triggered the collapsing of the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is probable, it is possible. If several shells were shot and if some of the shells were shot in a grouped way, yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question about tracer bullets had a purpose. On that video recording I mentioned earlier we can see traces of bullets hitting the bridge. You're a former JNA lieutenant-colonel, you're an expert in artillery matters; therefore, you should know that when there are fires, somebody establishes coordinates and those tracer bullets can show the people who fire where to shoot. So if there's an accumulation of explosives over time, there could be a breach that caused the bridge to collapse at one point. When I asked you whether you had access to material relating to the proceedings against the tank crew, I wanted to know whether the time element and the number were taken into account. Unfortunately, we did not have access to the material in those proceedings, but we would like to know what instructions were given to the tank crew and how they directed their fires, how they aimed. Was it haphazard or was it well-directed? Was there somebody for each and every fire? Was there someone directing it to make sure that the shell would hit the bridge? We do not have that element because the Prosecution did not adduce it, therefore we do not know it. That is the reason why I wanted to know whether you had access to the material in those proceedings. Don't you think it was the accumulation of shells that made the -- that eventually made the bridge to collapse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I mentioned, I had no contact with those documents, I did not have access to them. Fire correction is made for artillery -- field artillery. Tanks fire directly and correct automatically. That is the practice. So you have to take that into account when you view our analysis. I suppose, however, that those who were firing - I don't know why, I haven't thought about it - all I can say is that upon viewing those recordings when I saw those projectiles hitting several points I was not under the impression that they were aiming at the same point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] T-55 is a tank of Soviet make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it computerized or was it an old model?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot really tell you, but I work on computerized artillery systems and I believe that this particular tank was a mechanical one, it did not have computerized elements in itself, it was not composed of anything that was computerized inside. I'm not certain of this. As far as I remember, while I was working for the army of the former JNA I can tell you this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you've told us that the projectiles were not piercing bullets but explosive bullets. Just to be absolutely clear on this, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber where do you get this information? Why can you affirm with certainty that no projectile, no piercing projectiles, were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not an information that I have; it's my conclusion, it's the conclusion that I get when I look at the video-clip, when I see the explosion, when I see the little pieces of rock fall in the water. This is the conclusion I draw. If it had been a piercing shell, it would have just lodged itself inside the bridge construction. That's the effect it would create.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just to conclude this particular discussion, I think we're getting ahead of ourselves but then of course it helps, doesn't it? Professor, when you say "I didn't see that projectile," because that's what you were being asked, what exactly do you mean? Do you mean over a certain time just before the bridge collapsed? What is the time over which this occurs? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it and I repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question here on line 22 is: What exactly do you mean? Had it ended there, that would have been an appropriate open-ended question, but the further comments make it a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I merely summed up what the witness had said before and in no uncertain terms I'm just trying to draw everyone's attention to the time interval that is at stake. I think the witness should be allowed to go ahead and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let me repeat. If the projectile had destroyed the bridge, if it had caused the collapse of the bridge, in the same video sequence the frame just before the collapse, in that frame we should have seen that projectile, just like we have seen the projectiles on the other frames. Because from one frame to the next the projectile runs approximately 30 metres. So if one frame shows the collapse of the bridge when the projectile hit it, the previous frame should have shown the projectile. That's it. And we looked for it but we have not found that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand what you're saying, but did you yourself, as well as your colleagues, were you able to view image by image, second by second, footage by footage all the images to check if in the interval before the collapse, a projectile was actually hitting the bridge? Did you do that kind of work? Did you do that frame by frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we've proceeded exactly the way you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you have not noticed any shells, any projectile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none. No, none in the footage that we have, that we viewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many images per second are in a frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 24 seconds -- 24 images per second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Praljak wishes to take the floor. Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much. Can you please ask Mr. Jankovic not second by second, but the TV image where you have a split screen, 25 frames a second as opposed to the clip with 24 frames per second. Can you please ask the witness if they were actually using 25 frames per second when they were drawing up this analysis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what we said. We talked about 25 frames per second, and we analysed frame by frame. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have not seen any projectiles, any shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely none on the frames that we've analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think maybe I shouldn't be asking any additional questions, but even so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your last reply to the President you say you did not see any shells in the frames that you studied. Is this answer just about a certain time interval from the time of the destruction and then before that moment? Is that what your answer is actually in reference to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat once again. What is really important to understand and to see is the frame before the collapse occurs, that's what's important to analyse. So once again, the frame that precedes the collapse. This is where that projectile should have been visible. So the most important frame is the frame that just precedes the collapse of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is now perfectly clear. Professor, let us try to pick up where we left off -- or perhaps I should try and remind you. As soon as you ascertained that there was no impact by a shell in the period preceding the destruction of the bridge, what were the next steps you took from there and what were your assumptions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see in slow motion the collapse of the bridge, ORF2, and we could also view in slow motion the video-clip of our trial, of our experiment, in order to see the analogy between the water gush, pillar, wall, that is created in this exercise by detonating the cord and to compare this to what we see the water gush that is visible on the ORF2 footage, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we deal with that question, though, I would like to go back to the bridge which collapses following an impact by a shell. While I looked at your CV I was able to notice that you are a specialist in missiles. Hypothetically, let's say that if today we wanted to destroy the Old Bridge which was reconstructed and we actually walked on it, this Bench was able to walk on that bridge, we went there. If one wanted to destroy this bridge today would a MILAN missile or other type of missiles, would that be a thing that could make the bridge collapse immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A missile such as a MILAN missile would not be sufficient because it does not contain a sufficient amount of explosive, but there are missiles that were specially made for destroying these bridges. The former Yugoslavia had a missile called the Grom and it contained 50 kilogrammes of explosive and that one was actually made to destroy bridges of any type of construction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you had Grom at the time and that Grom missile would have been able to be destroy such a construction but it was not used, to your knowledge, for this particular case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to your calculations which are very well done, one needs approximately 50 kilogrammes in order to destroy a bridge made in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I must tell -- correct -- make a small correction. A charge of 50 kilometres [as interpreted], not at least 50 kilometres but 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Presiding Judge as well as the witness to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my fellow Judge just reminded me to slow down. Indeed, I shall. So one would need a detonation or a charge of 50 kilogrammes minimum. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to what is the minimum, that's difficult to answer. 50 kilogrammes would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The angle and the impact is also important, right, on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. It depends on many things, not only the angle but also the way the bridge is made, what the bridge is made of. There are also various sides of the bridge. Not every side of the bridge is vulnerable the same way and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that it is a quarter to 4.00. It is probably the right time to take a break. We did not see time go by, it just flew. Do you have any -- do you mind if we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a 20-minute break and we'll resume in 20 minutes' time. --- Break taken at 3.43 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. Mr. Kovacic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, I think we've covered most of your explanations and analysis in the questions and answers that we've done. Could you please move on now to the explanation of the elements in the comparison of what we see in the experiment, the test video in relation to one or both video-clips that were recorded live, the Mostar video and the ORF2 video. So what elements support the conclusion that you made and that you presented to us at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to three factors. First, there's this water gush or this wall of water, as the Presiding Judge named it; second factor --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a brusque movement and third factor, there is black smoke. We're going to see the three factors very clearly in the ORF2 recording. The light spot is not to be seen on the Mostar, TV Mostar, recording because it's over-lighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor Jankovic, you don't have the earphones, but the interpreters have indicated they have not understood the second factor.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The light spot or point. I shall repeat. First, you have this water gush or wall; secondly, this light spot, point, that appears suddenly and then disappears; third factor, the black smoke. One very relevant thing also is to notice this. When we see these facts, what is the order among themselves? Let's look at the recording. In slow motion we're going to watch ORF2, that footage, and we'll see that the water gush and the water gush we had in the test are basically the same, so the cause could be the same, if you agree to us viewing it. Can we show it in slow motion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see this water gush, please be watchful and look at it carefully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next to the water line, at the bottom of the bridge, on the eastern pillar, you can see a light spot for a very brief moment. Then, following the light spot, you can see black smoke. It is important to note that we first see the light spot, that's the very first thing, and then the water gushing, and then together with the water the black smoke. Can we now view in slow motion the experiment recording?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to make sure of one thing. That black smoke is on the right and the light spot on the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There where the light was you see the black smoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was left, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe can we see this footage again to make sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In slow motion, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my assistant is trying to pin-point the location with the cursor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please note exactly where in the bridge the light spot can be seen. I do ask you to be careful because this is precisely where the breach is going to form and this is precisely there where the bridge is going to collapse. On the right-hand side, you can see that the right-hand side remained standing, whilst the left part of the bridge is going to collapse. I shall repeat for the interpreters. On the right of the light spot, the part of the bridge on the right of the light spot remains standing, whilst the left part collapses. So it is that spot of light that is the border, the limit. Let's just wait until the smoke disappears and you'll see what is left of the bridge and then you'll see the right-hand side of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert, we see this light spot, it was shown with the cursor, the pointer. What does it correspond to? Is that the explosive exploding then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see what we found during the experiment and then we'll have an answer to your question. Please show us the test recording in slow motion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we've positioned the cord under the water, 50 centimetres below the surface of the water. On the right-hand side we activated, we ignited, the explosion of the detonating cord; on the left we positioned an explosive charge. Can you see the analogy? Have you found the answer to your question? It is relevant to see that the dot or spot of light is before the water wall, because the detonation occurs along the cord at a very high speed, 6.000 metres per second. Before the water rises, the explosive charge is ignited, is initiated. And then, after the spot of light, you can see the black smoke. What you can see here during the test is exactly what you can see on the -- in the ORF2 footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you reconstructed the event. What was your explosive charge? What was the power of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very small, 200 grams of TNT.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Mr. Kovacic, for taking the floor. Now I simply would like to ask the witness about the following, that what we have seen just now several times, the -- it was, of course, the very last phase of the collapse of the bridge. I wonder if the same -- in the same picture if you have something to show when the bridge was still standing. What struck me was that now we do not see any remnants of the bridge on the two sides, I mean on the left and the right, only what we see, of course, the position and the -- what is being caused by the explosives there. So I wonder if the very picture could be shown again including what happened beforehand, what happened prior to the -- to the collapse of the bridge, and then that picture which you kindly showed to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that would, in fact, be the ORF2 tape and the Mostar videotape but not in slow motion, the ones that we identified at the beginning. So we can perhaps show it now, first the ORF2 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then again the Mostar video, the quality is less there because it's been overexposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, there is a question that comes to my mind when we're looking at this footage, the ORF2 footage, because it's apparent that it is much better quality. In your work as you did this frame-by-frame analysis, this methodology that you applied, what was the key material that you used, that you relied on, as you did your analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: The ORF2 footage showed us much more because the TV Mostar is overexposed and the camera is shaking a lot, so it was difficult to analyse the footage. Still, it is possible to see all these elements but for the light of spot, and we therefore think that it's important footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I have a follow-up question. As regards the continuity on both recordings, is there a correlation between the Mostar video and the ORF2 recording? Did this increase the value of the material for the purposes of your analysis? So is there a correlation for purposes of triangulation, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: When you move from a frame to the next, we know what movements could have been done in that interval. And if you look at the ORF2 footage, the impression is that two pieces of footage have been glued or pasted next to one another as if there was a camera filming up to the moment of collapse and the other one would have filmed the collapse itself. The impression is that the first part was filmed while somebody was handling the camera because you see the moves by the cameraman, and the second footage seems to be a fixed camera. That's all I can say. However, because of that, the second part, the second footage, is very important because that one was done in one go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I heard in the interpretation the third video. Are you referring to the Mostar video, so that would mean the second one. Okay. Thank you very much. Well, in light of these explanations and given that our time is limited, I believe that I have about ten minutes left. I would now like to go back to the conclusions of your analysis. You outlined your conclusion already, but could you please give us a very specific answer to the question that is mentioned in your conclusion. What caused the bridge to collapse in light of everything that we saw, was it a tank shell? Was it an explosion? A charge that was set inside the bridge? Or was there a third reason? Could you please give us your conclusion very specifically.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm now speaking on behalf of three members of the team, and we agreed that I would state here that it is highly probable that the bridge was destroyed by an explosive charge. It is highly probable that it was destroyed by an explosive charge and not by a tank shell based on the recordings we viewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to keep track of the time. I think I have some ten minutes left, but I would now leave it up to you. Do you want to see the third video-clip, the experiment, once again so that you could do the comparison? I think that we've seen it enough times, but if you want you can ask for it to be played again. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary to view the experiment recording because we could see the light caused by the explosive charge, there's smoke, and then the water fountain, so there's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I also want to draw your attention to the fact that the parallel analysis of the video recordings, the ORF2 and Mostar video, that they were compared exhaustively in the analysis. So whoever wants to compare them even more can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So now after we've heard your conclusion I have another question. You were given a set of documents at the beginning of your testimony, so could you please look at document 3D 03154, it's the last document in this binder. Have you found it? Professor, have you seen this letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. You showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, you've read this letter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you've also read the CV of the author of the letter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you agree that Professor Hartmann, the author of this letter, he wrote this letter to me on the 30th of August. Is he a person who is qualified to speak about reasons for the destruction of buildings and constructions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see -- or with regard to building destruction by explosive, Professor Hartmann is certainly a highly qualified person. However, with regard to destruction of objects with projectiles, of course he is not a specialist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But is my understanding of your answer correct, you are suggesting that he is particularly qualified to study consequences of destruction, to judge any consequences or results of destruction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you at any point express a desire for a third party who you believed was sufficiently qualified to look at your study and perhaps offer up some criticism or advice, purely as a scientist? Was that instinctively your idea?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN JANKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed, even more than that we asked anybody who would be able to show us whatever that would be useful to better understand the issue would be welcome. That's what we said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, Mr. Praljak --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- had given us this booklet that he published on the destruction of the Old Mostar Bridge. And based on the reconstruction frame by frame and based on the experiment that you carried out, among scholars and scientists and experts in explosives or others, when the result of your research was published did scholars challenge the findings in other articles or was there no answer at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to our colleagues, I think that they all basically agreed. There was more noise, as it were, among politicians and journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But no scientist ever challenged your findings, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of our colleagues, and he's an old man, but he's -- still he's my student and he had a debate with me trying to contradict and challenge me. We discussed it, but he didn't manage to change my point of view. I can give you his name if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no need. Now, this water fountain or wall that we can see, does that respond to the cord that was, say, 50 centimetres or 1 metre under water and why this cord? Was it for the person activating the cord to be some distance away? Is that why we have the cord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see this water fountain rising over a certain distance. Could it be caused by a shell falling into the water and causing some splash, basically by sliding on the water it would cause the water to splash and cause this water fountain? I'm trying to thinks of all possibilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning of my career I often carried out firing sessions on the Adriatic coast. I had several shells sliding, gliding, on the water. It was not the case here. It doesn't look anything like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Judge Prandler first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel. Actually, Mr. Kovacic has already submitted a document here to you and to us under 3D 03154, 3D 03154. And it -- that one was a letter addressed to Mr. Bozidar Kovacic, and in that Professor Dietrich Hartmann from the Ruhr Universitaet Bochum has written an opinion about the issue and my question will be the following. According to the third paragraph in that letter, Professor Hartmann, about him you said that you were sure he was an expert and I quote the third paragraph: "According to the material available to me, the actual reasons for the collapse of the bridge are extremely uncertain. However, it is obvious to me that the tank shelling caused enormous destructions to the Old Bridge in Mostar. Insofar, for me it seems irrelevant whether a blasting has led to the final collapse of the bridge or not." And then in the very last sentence of his letter or opinion he says, and I quote again: "A definite statement on the reasons that caused the collapse at the end remains open." Now, my question is that in view of his expert opinion, let us say this, would you agree with his conclusions here which contained -- of course not only in the third paragraph and in the very last sentence which I -- which I quoted, but in his other parts of his own letter. So I would like to ask you if you would kindly comment on his views about the major causes of the collapse of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague Professor Hartmann does not know about the effects of projectiles. All he says is that they have caused major damage to the bridge, that's true. He also added that as far as he was concerned it was irrelevant to know what destroyed the bridge. We wanted to be more exact, more precise, and we concluded - I repeat with a high degree of probability - that the bridge was destroyed by an explosive. So it doesn't run counter to his opinion; it goes together, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this view. If it goes together, that is your opinion and his opinion, then it is then -- may -- may remain open, the question may remain open, what he explained here in his very last sentence that is: "A definite statement on the reason that caused the collapse at the end remains open," and, of course, you formulated your own view, that that is a high probability that finally the explosive charge was the reason. But I believe that you do not refuse his - I mean Professor Hartmann's - proposal and submission that the, and I quote again: " ... that the tank shelling caused enormous destructions to the Old Bridge in Mostar." And then he continued to say that it seemed to him irrelevant that a blasting has led to the final collapse of the bridge or not. So as far as I understood your conclusions, then you are both of the same view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the effects of projectiles, the effects on the bridge, I can say that the shelling damaged the bridge. Professor Hartmann I think, that's my opinion after viewing the recordings, the damages were -- occurred on the constructions added to the bridge, and those constructions were totally destroyed. The bridge itself was damaged. I do not know which term to use. It is better not to be too precise. I believe that Professor Hartmann is not qualified to talk about the destruction of the bridge caused by projectiles. With respect to the destruction of the bridge by projectiles, we both agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Jankovic, for your views and your explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I would like to ask you what could seem like a strange question. Most probably you won't have an answer to my question. I think it's necessary, however, to put that question to be complete. It seems that behind the assumption in question there is a theory that it was the Bosniaks which positioned a detonator and an explosive charge there. Have you ever discussed the matter? Was that matter ever raised during exchanges during your career?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very happy that you asked me that question. I can provide you with an answer, but this would not be a scientific answer. I can tell you what I know as a former military man. The Yugoslav tactic was such that all bridges were designed to be destroyed. I know that as a former officer. According to my opinion, it is highly probable that this explosive was a remnant of what was positioned there by the Yugoslav Army, but I refuse to say who activated the explosive. I refuse to say that, and my colleagues also said on several occasions that they can provide a technical point of view but they don't know who activated the charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think it is very right of you to say that. I didn't expect any other answer from you. The second part of your answer is interesting and it doesn't surprise me, because in my country it was just the same, all the bridges were designed to be destroyed if necessary. Does that include the detonating cord or was it only the explosive charge in the bridge, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not know that, I'm not certain about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very important issue, so we have to have an overview. Speaking of that detonating cord which could have been positioned under water and which was activated, in response to a question put by my fellow Judge you said that you'd rather not provide an opinion as to who activated the ignition. But as an expert, I will use the example of the bridge on the Kwai River, maybe you know about it. In that particular case we know that the bridge was under ABiH control. Was it possible for the HVO to send a diver with oxygen bottles who would have positioned the explosive charge at night, the detonating cord and the firing system, and then go back? Would it be possible that later on through an electronic system with a radio device could have activated the charge? Technically speaking, would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technically speaking, I think it is possible, but that's all I will say on the subject. I do not think that we had this technique at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
